claim: 76% of isolated Caco-2 cells spread circularly on a collagen-coated glass substrate, generating lamellipodia in all directions along the cell periphery with no persistent migration.
source: 76% of isolated Caco-2 cells spread circularly on a collagen-coated glass substrate, generating lamellipodia in all directions along the cell periphery with no persistent migration (Ozawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and cites a previous publication (Ozawa et al., 2020).

claim: In circularly spreading Caco-2 cells, nuclei exhibit rotational motion in a clockwise direction when viewed from the dorsal (apical) side.
source: In the cells spreading circularly, we noticed that the nuclei exhibit rotational motion in a clockwise direction when viewed from the dorsal (apical) side (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No Caco-2 cell exhibited rotational motion in a counterclockwise direction.
source: There was no cell that exhibited rotational motion in a counterclockwise direction.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The speed of nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells is about 50 degrees/hr on average.
source: The speed of nuclear rotation was about 50 degrees/hr on average (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The texture of the cytoplasm around the nucleus shows a rotating motion in the same direction as the nucleus.
source: The texture of the cytoplasm around the nucleus also showed a rotating motion, which indicates that the cytoplasm circulates in the same direction (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Microbeads attached to the dorsal surface of Caco-2 cells rotate.
source: Furthermore, we found that microbeads attached to the dorsal surface rotate (Video 2), confirming that the dorsal membrane also rotates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 2.

claim: The rotating motion of cell nuclei persists for more than 8 hr until cell division occurs.
source: The rotating motion of cell nuclei persists for more than 8 hr until cell division occurs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: After cell division, Caco-2 cells form two-cell colonies, and then the nuclear rotation resumes.
source: After the cell division, cells form two-cell colonies, and then the nuclear rotation resumes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The rotational speed of the nucleus depends on the type of coating applied to the glass substrate.
source: The rotational speed of the nucleus depended on the type of coating applied to the glass substrate, although the direction of rotation remained unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations comparing different substrate coatings.

claim: Caco-2 cells cultured on fibronectin-coated glass exhibit clockwise nuclear rotation at a slightly reduced speed compared to collagen-coated substrates.
source: When cells were cultured on fibronectin-coated glass, they exhibited the same clockwise nuclear rotation as observed on collagen-coated substrates, albeit at a slightly reduced speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: On poly-L-lysine-coated or uncoated glass, the rotation speed of Caco-2 cell nuclei further decreased, with some cells exhibiting little rotation.
source: On poly-L-lysine-coated or uncoated glass, the rotation speed further decreased, with some cells exhibiting little rotation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different substrate coatings influence the speed of nuclear rotation but do not alter its direction in Caco-2 cells.
source: Notably, while different coatings influenced the speed of nuclear rotation, they did not alter its direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations comparing different substrate coatings.

claim: In the peripheral region of Caco-2 cells, actin bundles are tilted, forming a dextral chiral pattern.
source: In the peripheral region of cells, actin bundles were tilted, forming a dextral chiral pattern (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Actin bundles in the peripheral region of Caco-2 cells associate with vinculin at their termini and are referred to as stress fibers.
source: Since each of these actin bundles appears to associate with vinculin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), a focal adhesion protein, at their termini, we refer to them as stress fibers (Tojkander et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cites a reference (Tojkander et al., 2012).

claim: In more interior regions of Caco-2 cells, actin filaments become thinner, lose their attachment to vinculin, and tend to adopt an orientation parallel to the cell periphery.
source: In more interior regions of the cell, actin filaments became thinner, losing their attachment to vinculin, and tended to adopt an orientation parallel to the cell periphery.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Microtubules in Caco-2 cells spread over the entire cytoplasmic region and exhibit a sinistral chiral pattern.
source: Microtubules spread over the entire cytoplasmic region and exhibited a sinistral chiral pattern (Figure 1D, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1D and Video 3.

claim: The sinistral pattern of microtubules in Caco-2 cells is consistent with the clockwise direction of nuclear rotation.
source: A similar sinistral pattern can emerge when filaments extend radially from a center and the central region rotates clockwise, which is consistent with the direction of nuclear rotation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern and the direction of nuclear rotation.

claim: Treatment with latrunculin A causes the shape of the Caco-2 cell periphery to become rough and nuclear rotation to stop.
source: When cells were treated with the actin polymerization inhibitor latrunculin A or F-actin stabilizer jasplakinolide, the shape of the cell periphery became rough and nuclear rotation stopped (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1, and Figure 2—video 2, respectively), indicating that F-actin is necessary for the nuclear and cytoplasmic rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: Treatment with jasplakinolide causes the shape of the Caco-2 cell periphery to become rough and nuclear rotation to stop.
source: When cells were treated with the actin polymerization inhibitor latrunculin A or F-actin stabilizer jasplakinolide, the shape of the cell periphery became rough and nuclear rotation stopped (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1, and Figure 2—video 2, respectively), indicating that F-actin is necessary for the nuclear and cytoplasmic rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 2.

claim: F-actin is necessary for the nuclear and cytoplasmic rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: When cells were treated with the actin polymerization inhibitor latrunculin A or F-actin stabilizer jasplakinolide, the shape of the cell periphery became rough and nuclear rotation stopped (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1, and Figure 2—video 2, respectively), indicating that F-actin is necessary for the nuclear and cytoplasmic rotation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with latrunculin A and jasplakinolide.

claim: Disruption of microtubules by nocodazole does not affect nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: In contrast, disruption of microtubules by nocodazole did not affect the nuclear rotation (Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—video 3), which indicates that microtubules are not involved in the rotating motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—video 3.

claim: Microtubules are not involved in the rotating motion of Caco-2 cells.
source: In contrast, disruption of microtubules by nocodazole did not affect the nuclear rotation (Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—video 3), which indicates that microtubules are not involved in the rotating motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with nocodazole.

claim: Treatment with CK666 causes lamellipodia at the cell periphery to shrink but nuclear rotation is maintained in Caco-2 cells.
source: When Caco-2 cells were treated with the Arp2/3 complex inhibitor CK666 (Nolen et al., 2009), lamellipodia at the cell periphery tended to shrink (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 4), but the nuclear rotation was maintained (Figure 2B, C), indicating that the Arp2/3 complex was dispensable for the rotating motion, in contrast to HFF where the Arp2/3 complex plays a role in cell chirality formation (Tee et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A, B, C, and Figure 2—video 4, and cites references (Nolen et al., 2009; Tee et al., 2015).

claim: The Arp2/3 complex is dispensable for the rotating motion in Caco-2 cells.
source: When Caco-2 cells were treated with the Arp2/3 complex inhibitor CK666 (Nolen et al., 2009), lamellipodia at the cell periphery tended to shrink (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 4), but the nuclear rotation was maintained (Figure 2B, C), indicating that the Arp2/3 complex was dispensable for the rotating motion, in contrast to HFF where the Arp2/3 complex plays a role in cell chirality formation (Tee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with CK666, and cites references (Nolen et al., 2009; Tee et al., 2015).

claim: In HFF cells, the Arp2/3 complex plays a role in cell chirality formation.
source: When Caco-2 cells were treated with the Arp2/3 complex inhibitor CK666 (Nolen et al., 2009), lamellipodia at the cell periphery tended to shrink (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 4), but the nuclear rotation was maintained (Figure 2B, C), indicating that the Arp2/3 complex was dispensable for the rotating motion, in contrast to HFF where the Arp2/3 complex plays a role in cell chirality formation (Tee et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tee et al., 2015.

claim: Treatment with SMIFH2 causes chiral stress fibers to mostly disappear in the peripheral regions of Caco-2 cells.
source: When cells were treated with this inhibitor, chiral stress fibers mostly disappeared in their peripheral regions, but instead, another pattern of F-actin appeared (Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 5.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, a subset of actin bundles become oriented in a radial direction.
source: Figure 3B shows that a subset of actin bundles became oriented in a radial direction, unlike the chiral pattern of stress fibers originally observed in the control cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, another population of F-actin is organized into a dense network or cluster with a concentric pattern.
source: Furthermore, another population of F-actin was organized into a dense network or cluster with a concentric pattern (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Despite the disappearance of peripheral chiral stress fibers in SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, the rotating motion is maintained.
source: Intriguingly, in spite of these drastic changes in the spatial organization of F-actin, and the disappearance of the peripheral chiral stress fibers, the rotating motion was maintained (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: In the first 5 hr of observation, the nuclear rotation speeds of control and SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells are comparable.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 2D, we noticed that, while the nuclear rotation speeds of control and SMIFH2-treated cells were comparable in the first 5 hr of the observation window, the nucleus of the SMIFH2-treated cells rotated significantly faster than control cells, on average, in the second 5 hr: the rotating speed of control cells slightly decreased over time, while SMIFH2-treated cells maintained or even slightly accelerated the rotating speed (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: In the second 5 hr of observation, the nucleus of SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells rotates significantly faster than control cells.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 2D, we noticed that, while the nuclear rotation speeds of control and SMIFH2-treated cells were comparable in the first 5 hr of the observation window, the nucleus of the SMIFH2-treated cells rotated significantly faster than control cells, on average, in the second 5 hr: the rotating speed of control cells slightly decreased over time, while SMIFH2-treated cells maintained or even slightly accelerated the rotating speed (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: The rotating speed of control Caco-2 cells slightly decreases over time.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 2D, we noticed that, while the nuclear rotation speeds of control and SMIFH2-treated cells were comparable in the first 5 hr of the observation window, the nucleus of the SMIFH2-treated cells rotated significantly faster than control cells, on average, in the second 5 hr: the rotating speed of control cells slightly decreased over time, while SMIFH2-treated cells maintained or even slightly accelerated the rotating speed (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells maintain or even slightly accelerate their rotating speed over time.
source: Furthermore, as shown in Figure 2D, we noticed that, while the nuclear rotation speeds of control and SMIFH2-treated cells were comparable in the first 5 hr of the observation window, the nucleus of the SMIFH2-treated cells rotated significantly faster than control cells, on average, in the second 5 hr: the rotating speed of control cells slightly decreased over time, while SMIFH2-treated cells maintained or even slightly accelerated the rotating speed (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: DIAPH2 and DAAM1 are highly expressed in Caco-2 cells.
source: Among the major mammalian formin family members (DIAPHs and DAAMs), DIAPH2 and DAAM1 were identified as being highly expressed in Caco-2 cells by RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Knockdown of DIAPH2 does not disrupt nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: However, knockdown of either DIAPH2 or DAAM1 did not disrupt nuclear rotation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D, Figure 2—videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D and Figure 2—videos 6 and 7.

claim: Knockdown of DAAM1 does not disrupt nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: However, knockdown of either DIAPH2 or DAAM1 did not disrupt nuclear rotation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D, Figure 2—videos 6 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D and Figure 2—videos 6 and 7.

claim: Formins are not essential for the chiral nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: These findings suggest that formins are not essential for the chiral nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells, in contrast to previous reports (Tee et al., 2015; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda et al., 2016; Abe and Kuroda, 2019; Middelkoop et al., 2021; Tee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with formin knockdown, and cites references (Tee et al., 2015; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda et al., 2016; Abe and Kuroda, 2019; Middelkoop et al., 2021; Tee et al., 2023).

claim: In DIAPH2 knockdown Caco-2 cells, the distribution of actin fibers is similar to that in control cells.
source: In DIAPH2 knockdown cells, the distribution of actin fibers was similar to that in control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, E' and Figure 2—video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, E' and Figure 2—video 6.

claim: A subset of DAAM1-knockdown Caco-2 cells display a detached end of the actin bundle, resembling the phenotype observed in SMIFH2-treated cells.
source: By contrast, a subset of DAAM1-knockdown cells displayed a detached end of the actin bundle, resembling the phenotype observed in SMIFH2-treated cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F, F' and Figure 2—video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F, F' and Figure 2—video 7.

claim: Treatment with blebbistatin causes the chiral pattern of peripheral F-actin to become less prominent in Caco-2 cells.
source: Under this condition, the chiral pattern of peripheral F-actin became less prominent (Figures 2A and 3C and Figure 2—video 8), while the nuclear rotation was mostly suppressed (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 2A, 3C, and Figure 2—video 8.

claim: Treatment with blebbistatin mostly suppresses nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: Under this condition, the chiral pattern of peripheral F-actin became less prominent (Figures 2A and 3C and Figure 2—video 8), while the nuclear rotation was mostly suppressed (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: Depletion of Myosin IIA and/or Myosin IIB heavy chains results in a significant reduction in nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: To confirm the role of Myosin II, we depleted Myosin IIA and/or Myosin IIB heavy chains in Caco-2 cells using siRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–D). Their depletion resulted in a significant reduction in the nuclear rotation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Figure 2—video 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B–D, and Figure 2—video 9.

claim: The activity of Myosin II is required for the chiral rotational motion in Caco-2 cells.
source: These results suggest that the activity of Myosin II is required for the chiral rotational motion and also for the formation of a chiral pattern of stress fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with blebbistatin and Myosin II depletion.

claim: The activity of Myosin II is required for the formation of a chiral pattern of stress fibers in Caco-2 cells.
source: These results suggest that the activity of Myosin II is required for the chiral rotational motion and also for the formation of a chiral pattern of stress fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with blebbistatin and Myosin II depletion.

claim: Both the activities of F-actin and Myosin II are important for nuclear and cytoplasmic rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: In summary, both the activities of F-actin and Myosin II are important for nuclear and cytoplasmic rotation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with various inhibitors and depletions.

claim: Nuclear rotation persists in Caco-2 cells even when chiral stress fibers are lost due to SMIFH2 treatment.
source: Our results using SMIFH2 showed that nuclear rotation persists even when the chiral stress fibers are lost, which suggests that these structures are not essential for driving rotational motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with SMIFH2.

claim: Chiral stress fibers are not essential for driving rotational motion in Caco-2 cells.
source: Our results using SMIFH2 showed that nuclear rotation persists even when the chiral stress fibers are lost, which suggests that these structures are not essential for driving rotational motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with SMIFH2.

claim: Upon vinculin depletion, the chiral arrangement of peripheral actin bundles is lost in Caco-2 cells.
source: Upon vinculin depletion, the chiral arrangement of peripheral actin bundles was lost. Nevertheless, the nucleus continued to rotate clockwise comparable to that observed in control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—video 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—video 10.

claim: Despite the loss of chiral arrangement of peripheral actin bundles upon vinculin depletion, the nucleus continues to rotate clockwise in Caco-2 cells.
source: Upon vinculin depletion, the chiral arrangement of peripheral actin bundles was lost. Nevertheless, the nucleus continued to rotate clockwise comparable to that observed in control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—video 10).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—video 10.

claim: Myosin II mediates chiral nuclear rotation through subcellular structures other than stress fibers in Caco-2 cells.
source: These results indicate that Myosin II mediates chiral nuclear rotation through subcellular structures other than stress fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with vinculin depletion.

claim: In the peripheral region of control Caco-2 cells, stress fibers localized on the ventral side exhibit a dextral swirling pattern.
source: In the peripheral region of the cell, stress fibers localized on the ventral side exhibited a dextral swirling pattern (yellow in the left panel and bold lines in the right panel of Figure 4A; red in Figure 4A'; dark red lines in Figure 5K, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4A, 4A', and Figure 5K.

claim: Peripheral stress fibers in control Caco-2 cells correspond to actin bundles associated with focal adhesions.
source: These peripheral stress fibers (red in Figure 4A') likely correspond to the actin bundles associated with focal adhesions, which were shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations shown in Figure 4A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adjacent to the inner edge of the peripheral cytoplasmic zone in control Caco-2 cells, actin filaments are oriented parallel to the cell periphery and lack obvious chirality.
source: Adjacent to the inner edge of the peripheral cytoplasmic zone having stress fiber bundles, we detected another population of actin filaments. These filaments, which looked thinner than stress fibers, were oriented parallel to the cell periphery and lacked obvious chirality, seemingly associated with the dorsal cell membranes (green in the left panel and dotted lines in the right panel of Figure 4A; light blue line in Figure 5K, top; green in Figure 4A').
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4A, 4A', and Figure 5K.

claim: Dorsal actin filaments in control Caco-2 cells are seemingly associated with the dorsal cell membranes.
source: Adjacent to the inner edge of the peripheral cytoplasmic zone having stress fiber bundles, we detected another population of actin filaments. These filaments, which looked thinner than stress fibers, were oriented parallel to the cell periphery and lacked obvious chirality, seemingly associated with the dorsal cell membranes (green in the left panel and dotted lines in the right panel of Figure 4A; light blue line in Figure 5K, top; green in Figure 4A').
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4A, 4A', and Figure 5K.

claim: Dorsal actin filaments in control Caco-2 cells likely correspond to those not anchored to focal adhesions.
source: These dorsal actin filaments (green in Figure 4A') likely correspond to those not anchored to the focal adhesions, which were detectable in the image of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations shown in Figure 4A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dorsal actin filaments in control Caco-2 cells do not associate with any other F-actin populations.
source: They also appeared not to associate with any other F-actin populations.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The distribution of Myosin IIA in control Caco-2 cells is similar to that of F-actin, except for its striped pattern.
source: Next, we examined the distribution of Myosin IIA using antibodies (Figure 4B). The distribution of Myosin IIA is similar to that of F-actin, except for its striped pattern.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: F-actin and Myosin IIA generally colocalize with one another in control Caco-2 cells.
source: Since we could not assess the colocalization of F-actin and Myosin IIA filaments in the same cells in ExM for technical reasons, we investigated their localization using conventional confocal microscopy (Figure 3A and Video 4). The confocal microscopy images indicate that F-actin and Myosin IIA generally colocalize with one another in these specimens.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3A and Video 4.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, chirally tilted actin stress fibers disappear at the peripheral region.
source: We next examined the distribution of F-actin and Myosin II in the cells treated with SMIFH2 (Figure 4C, C', D). As observed by conventional confocal microscopy, the chirally tilted actin stress fibers disappeared at the peripheral region, and instead, F-actin bundles extended radially from the cell edge toward its center (bold line in Figure 4C, right; dark red lines in Figure 5K, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4C, C', D, and Figure 5K.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, F-actin bundles extend radially from the cell edge toward its center.
source: We next examined the distribution of F-actin and Myosin II in the cells treated with SMIFH2 (Figure 4C, C', D). As observed by conventional confocal microscopy, the chirally tilted actin stress fibers disappeared at the peripheral region, and instead, F-actin bundles extended radially from the cell edge toward its center (bold line in Figure 4C, right; dark red lines in Figure 5K, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4C, C', D, and Figure 5K.

claim: In the interior region of SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, actin filaments are organized into a dense network with a concentric pattern, distributed at the dorsal side of cells.
source: In the interior region, actin filaments were organized into a dense network with a concentric pattern, which was distributed at the dorsal side of cells (green in the left and dotted lines in the right panels of Figure 4C; light blue line in Figure 5K, bottom; green in Figure 4C').
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4C, C', and Figure 5K.

claim: Myosin IIA exhibits a similar reorganization as F-actin in SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells.
source: Myosin IIA exhibited a similar reorganization as seen in F-actin (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: F-actin and Myosin IIA colocalize in SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, particularly in the concentric actin clusters.
source: As observed in control cells, confocal microscopy showed that F-actin and Myosin IIA also colocalize in the SMIFH2-treated cells, particularly in the concentric actin clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ExM analysis revealed more detailed features of actomyosin distribution, particularly detecting its concentric orientation, located more inside the cell than the peripheral stress fibers.
source: Thus, ExM analysis revealed more detailed features of actomyosin distribution, particularly detecting its concentric orientation, located more inside the cell than the peripheral stress fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ExM analysis.

claim: In blebbistatin-treated Caco-2 cells, the chiral orientation of stress fibers is greatly reduced in the peripheral region.
source: Additionally, we examined cells treated with blebbistatin by ExM, confirming the results obtained by live imaging and conventional immunostaining (Figures 2A and 3C). The chiral orientation of stress fibers was greatly reduced in the peripheral region after this treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In blebbistatin-treated Caco-2 cells, the dorsally located concentric actin filaments become undetectable.
source: Furthermore, the dorsally located concentric actin filaments became undetectable in these specimens.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Myosin II plays a complex role, including in the organization of dorsal actin filaments in Caco-2 cells.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that Myosin II plays a complex role, including in the organization of dorsal actin filaments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with blebbistatin.

claim: Stress fibers at the ventral side of control Caco-2 cells are almost immobile.
source: We found that stress fibers at the ventral side were almost immobile (Figure 5B), while the actin fibers at the dorsal side moved clockwise as indicated in snapshot images (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Actin fibers at the dorsal side of control Caco-2 cells move clockwise.
source: We found that stress fibers at the ventral side were almost immobile (Figure 5B), while the actin fibers at the dorsal side moved clockwise as indicated in snapshot images (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: F-actin bundles in the peripheral region with the chiral tilted pattern are almost immobile in control Caco-2 cells.
source: In Figure 5D, E, the kymographs along the green circle and the yellow line, which were analyzed at the ventral side, indicate that F-actin bundles in the peripheral region with the chiral tilted pattern are almost immobile (arrow in Figure 5D, Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5D, E, and Video 5.

claim: Along the dorsal cell membrane of control Caco-2 cells, the concentric actin filaments move clockwise while also moving centripetally.
source: To summarize, along the dorsal cell membrane, the concentric actin filaments move clockwise while also moving in centripetally (see also Video F-actin ring circulates along the dorsal membrane): we hereafter call this concentric structure 'the actomyosin ring' (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5F, G, and Video.

claim: The concentric structure of actin filaments moving clockwise and centripetally along the dorsal cell membrane is called 'the actomyosin ring'.
source: To summarize, along the dorsal cell membrane, the concentric actin filaments move clockwise while also moving in centripetally (see also Video F-actin ring circulates along the dorsal membrane): we hereafter call this concentric structure 'the actomyosin ring' (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors based on their observations.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, the actomyosin filaments organizing the ring move clockwise.
source: We also examined the dynamics of actin fibers in cells treated with SMIFH2, using live image data obtained by LLSM (Figure 5H–J). In Figure 5I, J, the kymographs along the red circle and yellow line (drawn in Figure 5H), respectively, indicate that the actomyosin filaments organizing the ring move clockwise (Figure 5I), and simultaneously flow centripetally (arrow 1 in Figure 5J), similar to the control condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, the actomyosin filaments organizing the ring simultaneously flow centripetally.
source: We also examined the dynamics of actin fibers in cells treated with SMIFH2, using live image data obtained by LLSM (Figure 5H–J). In Figure 5I, J, the kymographs along the red circle and yellow line (drawn in Figure 5H), respectively, indicate that the actomyosin filaments organizing the ring move clockwise (Figure 5I), and simultaneously flow centripetally (arrow 1 in Figure 5J), similar to the control condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, F-actin bundles radially extending from the cell periphery appear to move passively in a clockwise direction at their proximal ends.
source: Additionally, we found that in contrast to the immobile stress fibers with a chiral pattern in control cells (dark red lines in Figure 5K, top), F-actin bundles radially extending from the cell periphery in SMIFH2-treated cells appeared to move passively in a clockwise direction at their proximal ends, although they seem to keep the anchorage of the distal ends to the cell edge (arrow 2 in Figure 5J; Video 6 and dark red lines in Figure 5K, bottom), implying that these radial F-actin bundles do not play active roles in the chiral motion of the actin ring.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5J, Video 6, and Figure 5K.

claim: Radial F-actin bundles in SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells do not play active roles in the chiral motion of the actin ring.
source: Additionally, we found that in contrast to the immobile stress fibers with a chiral pattern in control cells (dark red lines in Figure 5K, top), F-actin bundles radially extending from the cell periphery in SMIFH2-treated cells appeared to move passively in a clockwise direction at their proximal ends, although they seem to keep the anchorage of the distal ends to the cell edge (arrow 2 in Figure 5J; Video 6 and dark red lines in Figure 5K, bottom), implying that these radial F-actin bundles do not play active roles in the chiral motion of the actin ring.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations shown in Figure 5J, Video 6, and Figure 5K.

claim: The concentric ring of flowing actomyosin filaments develops more extensively after SMIFH2 treatment in Caco-2 cells.
source: Thus, the concentric ring of flowing actomyosin filaments was detected also in the SMIFH2-treated cells but showing modified features (Figure 5K). Importantly, the ring developed more extensively after SMIFH2 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5K.

claim: The angular velocity is higher in the region where concentric actin filaments are present, rather than the region where actin blobs are present, in Caco-2 cells.
source: The spatial profile of the angular velocity (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H) indicates that it is higher in the region where concentric actin filaments are present, rather than the region where the actin blobs are present, indicating that the driving force could be present in the region of the actomyosin ring.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H.

claim: The driving force for rotation could be present in the region of the actomyosin ring in Caco-2 cells.
source: The spatial profile of the angular velocity (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H) indicates that it is higher in the region where concentric actin filaments are present, rather than the region where the actin blobs are present, indicating that the driving force could be present in the region of the actomyosin ring.
evidence: This is an inference based on PIV analysis shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H.

claim: The peak positions of individual angular velocity profiles are located around the scaled distance of one, which corresponds to the inner radius of the actomyosin ring.
source: We found that the peak positions of individual angular velocity profiles, as well as the peak positions of the angular velocity profiles averaged over samples, are located around the scaled distance of one, which suggests that the driving force is present in the region around the actomyosin ring.
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The driving force for rotation is present in the region around the actomyosin ring in Caco-2 cells.
source: We found that the peak positions of individual angular velocity profiles, as well as the peak positions of the angular velocity profiles averaged over samples, are located around the scaled distance of one, which suggests that the driving force is present in the region around the actomyosin ring.
evidence: This is an inference based on PIV analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In an SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cell, fluorescent debris that seemed to attach to the actomyosin ring persistently circulated approximately three times as fast as the rotating speed of the nucleus.
source: We additionally observed another interesting phenomenon to support our idea. In an SMIFH2-treated cell that was imaged by a conventional fluorescence confocal microscope (LSM880, Zeiss), we, by chance, observed that fluorescent debris that seemed to attach to the actomyosin ring persistently circulated approximately three times as fast as the rotating speed of the nucleus: ∼400 and ∼140 degrees/hr for the debris and nucleus, respectively. (Figure 6—video 2, yellow and white lines, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6—video 2.

claim: The actomyosin ring generates a driving force for rotating the nucleus and cytoplasm in Caco-2 cells.
source: These observations support the notion that the actomyosin ring generates a driving force for rotating the nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from observations of fluorescent debris circulation.

claim: The PIV analysis for F-actin dynamics may underestimate the flow velocity in Caco-2 cells.
source: Note that, since the angular velocity estimated from the motion of debris was faster than that obtained from the PIV analysis, our PIV analysis for F-actin dynamics may underestimate the flow velocity.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing angular velocities from debris motion and PIV analysis.

claim: The actomyosin ring is a cell-scale structure that drives the chiral cytoplasmic flow in Caco-2 cells.
source: Our observations indicate the possibility that the actomyosin ring is a cell-scale structure that drives the chiral cytoplasmic flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations.

claim: The rotational motion of the actomyosin ring should be driven solely through its own mechanism, without relying on other structures.
source: Since the actin filaments of the ring seemed not to have contact with the peripheral stress fibers in control cells, their rotational motion should be driven solely through its own mechanism, without relying on other structures, contrasted with the previous model that the contact between transverse fibers and radial fibers plays a role in establishing the cell chirality in HFF (Tee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations and cites a reference (Tee et al., 2015).

claim: In HFF, the contact between transverse fibers and radial fibers plays a role in establishing cell chirality.
source: Since the actin filaments of the ring seemed not to have contact with the peripheral stress fibers in control cells, their rotational motion should be driven solely through its own mechanism, without relying on other structures, contrasted with the previous model that the contact between transverse fibers and radial fibers plays a role in establishing the cell chirality in HFF (Tee et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tee et al., 2015.

claim: The theoretical model demonstrates that the observed cell-scale unidirectional rotation is driven by the molecular-scale chirality of actomyosin filaments even in the absence of cell-scale chiral orientational order.
source: This model demonstrated that the observed cell-scale unidirectional rotation is driven by the molecular-scale chirality of actomyosin filaments even in the absence of cell-scale chiral orientational order.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical model.

claim: The sinistral swirling pattern at the dorsal side in the theoretical model is driven by both centripetal and clockwise flows.
source: The sinistral swirling pattern at the dorsal side shown in Figure 7F is driven by both centripetal and clockwise flows, which were indeed observed by LLSM shown in Figure 5.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical model and experimental observations shown in Figure 7F and Figure 5.

claim: The dextral swirling pattern of the flow on the ventral side in the theoretical model is consistent with the chiral pattern of the stress fibers on the ventral side.
source: Interestingly, the dextral swirling pattern of the flow on the ventral side is consistent with the chiral pattern of the stress fibers on the ventral side (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a comparison between the theoretical model and experimental observations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The dextral chiral pattern of the stress fibers on the ventral side is self-organized through alignment with the fluid flow.
source: When the chiral flow was inhibited with blebbistatin, such a chiral pattern at the ventral side disappeared (Figures 2A and 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the ventral chiral tilted patterns are indeed formed in a flow-dependent manner. This implies that the dextral chiral pattern of the stress fibers is self-organized through alignment with the fluid flow on the ventral side.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations with blebbistatin shown in Figures 2A, 3C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The actomyosin ring located at the dorsal side of Caco-2 cells plays a key role in the rotating motion.
source: Our experimental observations and theoretical results suggest that the actomyosin ring located at the dorsal side of Caco-2 cells plays a key role in the rotating motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations and theoretical results.

claim: Treatment with Rho Activator II results in a substantial increase in the thickness and number of actomyosin bundles at the ventral side in Caco-2 cells.
source: Remarkably, we observed a substantial increase in the thickness and number of actomyosin bundles at the ventral side, particularly beneath the nucleus, in Caco-2 cells treated with Rho Activator II, while the dorsal actomyosin appeared to decrease significantly (Figure 8A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8A, C.

claim: Treatment with Rho Activator II causes the dorsal actomyosin to decrease significantly in Caco-2 cells.
source: Remarkably, we observed a substantial increase in the thickness and number of actomyosin bundles at the ventral side, particularly beneath the nucleus, in Caco-2 cells treated with Rho Activator II, while the dorsal actomyosin appeared to decrease significantly (Figure 8A, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8A, C.

claim: The ratio of dorsal to ventral actomyosin is reduced significantly in Caco-2 cells treated with Rho Activator II compared with control cells.
source: The ratio of dorsal to ventral actomyosin was reduced significantly in the cell treated with Rho Activator II compared with control cells (Figure 8D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8D, E.

claim: The rotational motion of the nucleus ceases in Caco-2 cells treated with Rho Activator II.
source: We then performed live imaging of Caco-2 cells treated with Rho Activator II and found that the rotational motion of the nucleus ceased (Figure 8—video 1), supporting the idea that the dorsal actomyosin is crucial for driving the rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8—video 1.

claim: The dorsal actomyosin is crucial for driving the rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: We then performed live imaging of Caco-2 cells treated with Rho Activator II and found that the rotational motion of the nucleus ceased (Figure 8—video 1), supporting the idea that the dorsal actomyosin is crucial for driving the rotation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with Rho Activator II shown in Figure 8—video 1.

claim: In SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells, the dorsal actomyosin appears to increase, while the ventral actomyosin decreases.
source: On the other hand, in cells treated with SMIFH2, the dorsal actomyosin appeared to increase, while the ventral actomyosin decreased (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8A, B.

claim: The ratio of dorsal to ventral actomyosin in SMIFH2-treated Caco-2 cells tends to increase, although the difference is not statistically significant.
source: The ratio of dorsal to ventral actomyosin in cells treated with SMIFH2 tended to increase, although the difference was not statistically significant (Figure 8D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8D, E.

claim: Actomyosin at the dorsal side is crucial for driving rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: Taken together, our findings further support the idea that actomyosin at the dorsal side is crucial for driving rotation in Caco-2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with Rho Activator II and SMIFH2.

claim: Caco-2 cells exhibit nuclear rotation and cytoplasmic circulation clockwise when cultured as a single cell.
source: In this study, we investigated the mechanism underlying cell-scale chiral dynamics, which is observed in Caco-2 epithelial cells when cultured as a single cell. We found that Caco-2 cells exhibited nuclear rotation and cytoplasmic circulation clockwise, and these movements require actin and Myosin II activities.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Nuclear rotation and cytoplasmic circulation in Caco-2 cells require actin and Myosin II activities.
source: In this study, we investigated the mechanism underlying cell-scale chiral dynamics, which is observed in Caco-2 epithelial cells when cultured as a single cell. We found that Caco-2 cells exhibited nuclear rotation and cytoplasmic circulation clockwise, and these movements require actin and Myosin II activities.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The concentric actomyosin ring located on the dorsal side of Caco-2 cells moves in a clockwise direction.
source: High-resolution microscopy has revealed that the concentric actomyosin ring located on the dorsal side of the cells moves in a clockwise direction, leading us to hypothesize that this process may play a critical role in driving cytoplasmic flow.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The actomyosin ring by itself is moving in a clockwise direction through its own mechanism in Caco-2 cells.
source: In the case of Caco-2 cells, however, we did not detect such radial fibers crossing the concentric actomyosin ring, and our observations suggested that the actomyosin ring by itself was moving in a clockwise direction through its own mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The actomyosin localized under the dorsal membrane induces an active unidirectional fluid flow of the viscous cytoplasm and in turn nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells.
source: To test this idea, we employed active chiral fluid theory (Fürthauer et al., 2012; Fürthauer et al., 2013; Naganathan et al., 2014), showing that the actomyosin localized under the dorsal membrane induces an active unidirectional fluid flow of the viscous cytoplasm and in turn nuclear rotation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study and cites references (Fürthauer et al., 2012; Fürthauer et al., 2013; Naganathan et al., 2014).

claim: The nuclear rotation and cytoplasmic flow in Caco-2 cells is driven by the molecular-scale chiral mechanics of actomyosin rather than the cell-scale chiral orientation of actomyosin.
source: Since the concentric pattern of actomyosin has no chirality at the cellular scale, our theory indicates that the nuclear rotation and cytoplasmic flow in Caco-2 cells is driven by the molecular-scale chiral mechanics of actomyosin rather than the cell-scale chiral orientation of actomyosin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical model.

claim: No visible cytoskeletal linkage between the nucleus and other cellular structures was detected in Caco-2 cells.
source: It is also of note that we did not detect any visible cytoskeletal linkage between the nucleus and other cellular structures, another potential machinery for driving nuclear rotation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The nuclear rotation in Caco-2 cells may be induced directly by the cytoplasmic circulating flow mediated by the friction between the nuclear surface and the cytoplasm.
source: The nuclear rotation may be induced directly by the cytoplasmic circulating flow mediated by the friction between the nuclear surface and the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observations.

claim: Microtubules and the peripheral stress fibers in Caco-2 cells exhibited chiral distribution patterns, but there is no evidence that they are involved in the chiral motion of the nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Microtubules and the peripheral stress fibers also exhibited chiral distribution patterns, but we obtained no evidence that they are involved in the chiral motion of the nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations.

claim: The chiral distribution of microtubules and peripheral stress fibers in Caco-2 cells may have been generated as a result of the cytoplasmic flow mechanism.
source: It is, therefore, possible that their chiral distribution was generated as a result of the above-mentioned mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observations.

claim: Myosin II is involved in the chirality of Caco-2 cells.
source: Our experiments using an inhibitor and RNAi-mediated depletion have revealed that Myosin II is involved in the chirality of Caco-2 cells, which is consistent with previous studies showing the involvement of Myosin II in the chiral behaviors of several types of cells (Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations and cites a reference (Kumar et al., 2014).

claim: Formins are not required for Caco-2 cell chirality.
source: Interestingly, while some of these studies concluded that formins are essential for breaking the chiral symmetry (Tee et al., 2015; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda et al., 2016; Abe and Kuroda, 2019; Middelkoop et al., 2021; Tee et al., 2023), our results showed that the rotational speed in Caco-2 cells did not decrease but even slightly increased when treated with SMIFH2, a known inhibitor of formins, suggesting that formins are not required for Caco-2 cell chirality.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations and cites references (Tee et al., 2015; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda et al., 2016; Abe and Kuroda, 2019; Middelkoop et al., 2021; Tee et al., 2023).

claim: How cells respond to SMIFH2 depends on their types.
source: These reports suggest that how cells respond to SMIFH2 depends on their types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different studies.

claim: In Caco-2 cells treated with SMIFH2, the actomyosin ring becomes more visible than in the control cells.
source: In Caco-2 cells treated with SMIFH2, the actomyosin ring became more visible than in the control cells (Figures 3, 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figures 3, 4.

claim: Treatment by Rho Activator II increases stress fiber formation at the ventral side in Caco-2 cells.
source: In contrast, treatment by Rho Activator II increased the stress fiber formation at the ventral side, which can induce a shift of actin and Myosin II to the ventral side, leading to a decrease in the formation of actomyosin ring at the dorsal side (Figure 8D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 8D, E.

claim: Dorsal actomyosin constitutes the driving force behind the rotational motion in Caco-2 cells.
source: These considerations provide support for the model that dorsal actomyosin constitutes the driving force behind the rotational motion, as the rotation tended to increase or decrease in SMIFH2- or Rho Activator II-treated cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations with SMIFH2 and Rho Activator II.

claim: Zebrafish melanophores exhibit a counterclockwise nuclear rotation from basement view.
source: Several types of cells have been reported to exhibit chiral nuclear rotation. Zebrafish melanophores exhibit a counterclockwise nuclear rotation 'from basement view' (Yamanaka and Kondo, 2015), which is the same as our observation where the nucleus rotates in a clockwise direction viewed from the dorsal side.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamanaka and Kondo, 2015.

claim: Actin plays a pivotal role in the chiral rotational motion in zebrafish melanophores.
source: The study reported that actin plays a pivotal role in the chiral rotational motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study on zebrafish melanophores.

claim: Singly isolated MDCK cells embedded in a 3D culture exhibit rotations in either direction with a bias to the counterclockwise direction.
source: In the case of singly isolated MDCK cells embedded in a 3D culture, nuclei as well as whole cells exhibited rotations in either direction with a bias to the counterclockwise direction (Chin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chin et al., 2018.

claim: A weak inhibition of actin polymerization reverses the bias in the rotational motion in MDCK cells.
source: Furthermore, a weak inhibition of actin polymerization reversed the bias in the rotational motion, and an actin-binding protein α-actinin-1 regulates the direction of chiral rotation (Chin et al., 2018), similar to the case of HFF (Tee et al., 2015; Tee et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chin et al., 2018.

claim: α-actinin-1 regulates the direction of chiral rotation in MDCK cells.
source: Furthermore, a weak inhibition of actin polymerization reversed the bias in the rotational motion, and an actin-binding protein α-actinin-1 regulates the direction of chiral rotation (Chin et al., 2018), similar to the case of HFF (Tee et al., 2015; Tee et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chin et al., 2018.

claim: In C2C12 myoblasts, whether actin filaments are organized or disorganized correlates with chirally biased nuclear rotation.
source: In the case of C2C12 myoblasts, whether actin filaments were organized or disorganized was shown to correlate with chirally biased nuclear rotation (Kwong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kwong et al., 2019.

claim: The mechanism of cell chirality formation differs between HFF and Caco-2 cells.
source: In contrast to HFF (Tee et al., 2015; Tee et al., 2023), the direction of nuclear rotation of Caco-2 is opposite and the chirality of Caco-2 does not require the activity of Arp2/3 complex (Figure 2) nor physical interactions between the actin ring and other actin structures such as radial fibers. Thus, the mechanism of cell chirality formation seems to differ between cell types, such as HFF and Caco-2 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental observations with previous studies and cites references (Tee et al., 2015; Tee et al., 2023).

claim: Beads attached externally to the dorsal membrane of Caco-2 cells exhibit both chiral rotation and centripetal movement.
source: Beads attached externally to the dorsal membrane exhibited both chiral rotation and centripetal movement, as shown in Video 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 2.

claim: The dorsal membrane of Caco-2 cells moves in concert with the underlying actomyosin.
source: This behavior mirrors the movement of actin filaments at the dorsal side, suggesting that the dorsal membrane moves in concert with the underlying actomyosin.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of bead movement.

claim: The ventral membrane of Caco-2 cells is likely immobile.
source: In contrast, stress fibers located just above the ventral membrane did not move as shown in the leftmost panel of Video 5, suggesting that the ventral membrane is likely immobile.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations shown in Video 5.

claim: The dorsal region of Caco-2 cells undergoes twisting relative to the ventral region.
source: These observations imply that the dorsal region of the cell undergoes twisting relative to the ventral region.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of membrane movement.

claim: Similar twisting behavior has been observed in zebrafish melanophores.
source: Similar twisting behavior has been observed in zebrafish melanophores (Yamanaka and Kondo, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamanaka and Kondo, 2015.

claim: Changes in rotational speed with substrate coating may be attributed to redistribution of actomyosin or substrate-dependent changes in the cell's internal physical environment.
source: The observation that rotational speed changes with substrate coating (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) may be attributed to several factors, including redistribution of actomyosin that affects the amount of dorsal actomyosin, as exemplified by the effect of Rho Activator II, and substrate-dependent changes in the cell's internal physical environment, such as variations in effective viscosity at the ventral side.
evidence: This is a speculation based on observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A tissue-scale asymmetry, such as a spatial gradient in the strength of cell-scale torque generation, is necessary for tissue-scale left–right asymmetry to arise from cell chirality.
source: Our previous theoretical studies showed that a tissue-scale asymmetry, such as a spatial gradient in the strength of cell-scale torque generation, is necessary for the tissue-scale left–right asymmetry to arise from cell chirality (Yamamoto et al., 2020; Sato et al., 2015b; Sato et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical studies (Yamamoto et al., 2020; Sato et al., 2015b; Sato et al., 2015a).
